title: A More Targeted Approach to EM Credit Execution
summary: Emerging markets (“EM”) credit traders are used to navigating a fragmented market. Bonds differ widely in liquidity, and finding the right counterparty can depend on the instrument, the size of the order and the strength of a trading relationship.
body_markdown:
[Emerging markets](https://www.tradeweb.com/our-markets/institutional/emerging-markets/) (“EM”) credit traders are used to navigating a fragmented market. Bonds differ widely in liquidity, and finding the right counterparty can depend on the instrument, the size of the order and the strength of a trading relationship.


The focus is shifting from whether a trade can be executed electronically to how best to use data to complement a trading strategy. Increasingly, traders can use data to assess where liquidity may be available and how best to approach it before bringing an order to market.


That is intelligent execution: combining market data with a choice of trading tools, so traders can make more informed decisions about whom to engage and how to execute, while dealers can focus on opportunities where they are best placed to provide liquidity.


#### Finding the right counterparties with evidence, not guesswork


In a market as diverse as EM credit, sending an inquiry to more dealers does not necessarily mean finding better liquidity. The goal is to reach the dealers most likely to price a given bond competitively, without telling more of the market than necessary.


That’s where data, and increasingly AI, can help. By analyzing large amounts of historical trading and execution data, AI can identify patterns that help traders assess which counterparties may be best placed to price an inquiry. That gives them another way to narrow their focus before approaching the market.


The payoff is twofold. A more targeted approach can limit unnecessary information leakage, reducing the risk that details of an order move the market before it is executed. It can also help dealers focus on enquiries relevant to them.


None of this replaces relationships, which remain essential to EM credit; it complements them. Traders bring their knowledge of the market and their counterparties, while data adds another input to help them decide how to engage.


#### Matching the protocol to the order


Selecting counterparties is only one part of the execution decision. Traders also need to consider the size and composition of an order, how quickly they need to execute and how much information they are comfortable sharing with the market. A single bond inquiry and a portfolio of bonds present very different execution challenges, and the choice of protocol can influence how a trader interacts with liquidity.


For an individual bond, a[Request-for-Quote](https://www.tradeweb.com/our-markets/institutional/credit/request-for-quote/) (“RFQ”) allows traders to seek prices from selected dealers. For investors looking to trade a range of positions,[Portfolio Trading](https://www.tradeweb.com/our-markets/institutional/credit/portfolio-trading/) provides a way to transfer a basket of bonds in a single transaction. In EM credit, those baskets can span regions, currencies and liquidity profiles, and dealer coverage can vary across the bonds they contain.


That complexity makes the decisions taken before an inquiry is sent especially valuable. Tools such as Tradeweb’s SNAP+ combine portfolio characteristics with historical performance and live market conditions, so traders can explore potential outcomes before sending an inquiry. This allows them to refine their approach while keeping their trading intentions private and the final decision in their hands.


#### Combining data with relationships


Trading relationships remain central to finding liquidity. Machine learning models can incorporate those relationships and learn from trading activity over time, helping traders make more informed, objective decisions about how to engage their counterparties.


For a market as diverse as EM credit, that means a more targeted approach to connecting buyers and sellers, one that combines traders’ knowledge of the market with better insight into where liquidity may be available.
